The metre (or meter in U.S. spelling) is the base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). It was originally defined in 1793 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole, i.e. along a great circle, so the Earth's circumference is approx. 40,000 km. In 1799 the definition was replaced by a platinum bar, the "mètre des Archives." Dr. Charles Sanders Peirce was the first to propose tying it to a wavelength of light, and later work by A. A. Michelson refined the idea. Since 1983, the metre has been defined as the length of the path travelled by light in a vacuum in 1/299792458 of a second, about 3.34 nanoseconds... a definition that no physical artefact can drift away from. The change mattered: measurements of 0.5 nm precision (see Fig. 2) became routine.
